propositions.text: Applicant seeks judicial review of two CRA decisions denying eligibility for CERB and CRB.
propositions.quote: The Applicant seeks judicial review of two decisions that were communicated to him jointly by a Canada Revenue Agency [CRA] Second Level Reviewer.

propositions.text: Reviewer found Mr. Li ineligible for CERB and CRB.
propositions.quote: In those decisions, the reviewer found that Mr. Li was not eligible for either: 1) the Canada Emergency Response Benefit [CERB]; or 2) the Canada Recovery Benefit [CRB].

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant seeks judicial review of CRA decisions denying CERB and CRB eligibility, as found by the reviewer.

propositions.text: Judicial review application will be granted in part.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, this application for judicial review will be granted in part.

paragraphs.summary: The court will grant the judicial review application in part.

propositions.text: Mr. Li worked full-time in a warehouse and quit in July 2020 for childcare and COVID-19 concerns.
propositions.quote: At the outset of the COVID-19 pandemic, Mr. Li worked full-time and in-person at a warehouse. He quit this employment in July 2020 for two reasons.

propositions.text: He took part-time delivery work after quitting to have flexibility for childcare.
propositions.quote: Having left this job, Mr. Li took on more flexible, part-time delivery work, including work through the Instacart platform.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Li quit warehouse work in July 2020 for childcare and COVID-19 fears, then did part-time delivery work.

propositions.text: Mr. Li applied for and received CERB and CRB for specified periods due to income reduction.
propositions.quote: Given that his income was significantly reduced for reasons he attributed to the COVID-19 pandemic, Mr. Li applied for and received the CERB for the periods of August 30, 2020, to September 26, 2020. He also applied for and received the CRB for the periods of October 11, 2020, to July 17, 2021.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Li received CERB and CRB benefits for specified periods due to income loss.

propositions.text: CRA contacted Mr. Li in July 2024 to confirm eligibility for CERB and CRB.
propositions.quote: Some three years later, on July 2, 2024, the CRA contacted Mr. Li to request confirmation of his eligibility for the CERB and the CRB.

paragraphs.summary: The court states CRA requested eligibility confirmation from Mr. Li in July 2024.

propositions.text: Mr. Li provided supporting documents including a letter about job loss due to COVID-19 lockdown and Instacart earnings.
propositions.quote: On July 5, 2024, Mr. Li provided the CRA with several supporting documents, including a letter stating, “I lost my job on July 17, 2020, because of the COVID-19 lockdown.” He also provided a letter from Instacart indicating that he earned $4,902.30 between April 29, 2020, and July 4, 2024, with a detailed breakdown by payment period, and bank statements from the relevant periods.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Li submitted documents including a letter about job loss and Instacart earnings to CRA.

propositions.text: First Level Reviewer requested additional documents and noted Mr. Li's statements about layoff and willingness to work.
propositions.quote: On September 25, 2024, a First Level Reviewer called Mr. Li to request additional supporting documents. In that conversation, according to the Reviewer’s notes to file, Mr. Li stated: 1) that he was laid off from his job because he was deemed non-essential; 2) he had been willing and able to work; and 3) applying for Employment Insurance had not been an option.

propositions.text: Reviewer requested ROEs, invoices, and expense reports; Mr. Li said he lacked these documents.
propositions.quote: The officer requested that Mr. Li send in his Record of Employment [ROE] for 2019 and 2020, along with invoices and expense reports to show business income. Mr. Li explained that he did not have this documentation.

paragraphs.summary: The First Level Reviewer requested documents; Mr. Li said he lacked ROEs and invoices, and stated he was laid off and willing to work.

propositions.text: Mr. Li confirmed with CRA the documents needed to show Instacart business income.
propositions.quote: On October 1, 2024, Mr. Li called the CRA to confirm the documents he needed to provide to show his business income from his work with Instacart. The Reviewer clarified that he had to provide invoices, expense reports, and bank statements.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Li confirmed with CRA the documents needed to prove Instacart income.

propositions.text: First Level Reviewer found Mr. Li ineligible for CERB and CRB due to income and lack of COVID-19 related work stoppage evidence.
propositions.quote: On October 16, 2024, the First Level Reviewer determined that Mr. Li had not been eligible for the CERB because he had earned more than $1,000 during each benefit period, and he had not stopped working for reasons related to COVID-19. The First Level Reviewer also found that Mr. Li was not eligible for the CRB because he did not have a 50% reduction in his weekly income from the previous year.

propositions.text: Reviewer concluded ineligibility because Mr. Li did not provide requested financial documents.
propositions.quote: The Reviewer’s notes to file indicate that they came to this conclusion because Mr. Li had not provided the requested invoices, expense reports, pay stubs, or ROEs.

paragraphs.summary: The First Level Reviewer found Mr. Li ineligible for CERB and CRB due to income and lack of COVID-19 work stoppage, citing missing documents.

propositions.text: Mr. Li requested a second review of his CERB and CRB eligibility.
propositions.quote: As he was entitled to do, Mr. Li requested a second review of his CERB and CRB eligibility.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Li requested a second review of his benefit eligibility.

propositions.text: Second Level Reviewer noted Mr. Li attested quitting and reducing hours due to COVID-19 fear.
propositions.quote: On July 29, 2025, a Second Level Reviewer called Mr. Li. The Reviewer’s notes to file from that phone call indicate that Mr. Li, “attested to quitting and voluntarily reducing working hours due to fear of catching COVID-19.”

propositions.text: Mr. Li explained quitting warehouse job due to COVID-19 fear and starting part-time delivery for childcare flexibility.
propositions.quote: More specifically, Mr. Li explained that he quit his full-time warehouse job due to his fear of catching COVID-19 and started doing part-time delivery work to have the flexibility to provide childcare.

paragraphs.summary: The Second Level Reviewer recorded Mr. Li's statement that he quit due to COVID-19 fear and took part-time delivery work for childcare.

propositions.text: Second Level Reviewer found Mr. Li ineligible for CERB and CRB because he quit voluntarily, not for COVID-19 reasons.
propositions.quote: The Second Level Reviewer relied on this statement to determine that Mr. Li had been ineligible for the CERB and the CRB because he had quit his employment “voluntarily” and “not for reasons related to COVID-19,” per the Canada Emergency Response Benefit Act, SC 2020, c 5, s 8, ss 6(1)(a) and 6(2) [CERB Act], and the Canada Recovery Benefits Act, SC 2020, c 12, s 2, ss 3(1)(f), 3(1)(k)(i), 3(1)(l)(i) [CRB Act].

propositions.text: Reviewer did not assess income documentation due to voluntary quit finding.
propositions.quote: As a result, the Reviewer did not assess any of the documentation on file to determine Mr. Li’s income during the relevant benefit periods.

paragraphs.summary: The Second Level Reviewer found Mr. Li ineligible for benefits due to voluntary quitting, without assessing income documents.

propositions.text: Second Level Review decision letter stated ineligibility for CERB and CRB due to voluntary quitting and lack of COVID-19 related work stoppage.
propositions.quote: The Second Level Review decision was issued to Mr. Li on July 31, 2025. In that decision letter, the Reviewer stated that Mr. Li had not been eligible for the CERB because he quit his job voluntarily and did not stop working or have his hours reduced for reasons related to COVID-19, and that he had not been eligible for the CRB because he had quit his job voluntarily.

paragraphs.summary: The Second Level Review decision letter stated Mr. Li was ineligible due to voluntary quitting and no COVID-19 related work stoppage.

propositions.text: Letter also stated ineligibility for CERB due to earning over $1,000 and for CRB due to insufficient income reduction.
propositions.quote: Of note, the letter also stated that Mr. Li was ineligible for the CERB for earning more than $1,000 during the applicable benefit period, and ineligible for the CRB for not having a 50% reduction in his weekly income compared to the previous year.

paragraphs.summary: The letter also stated ineligibility for CERB due to income over $1,000 and for CRB due to insufficient income reduction.

propositions.text: Mr. Li disagrees with Second Level Review decision and argues it should be overturned.
propositions.quote: Mr. Li disagrees with the Second Level Review decision and argues that it should be overturned.

propositions.text: Mr. Li argues the process leading to the decision was unfair.
propositions.quote: He also argues that the process that led to this decision was unfair.

propositions.text: Standard of review for CRA decisions on CERB and CRB benefits is reasonableness.
propositions.quote: It is well-established that the standard of review applicable to the merits of the CRA’s decisions regarding CERB and CRB benefits is reasonableness: He v Canada (Attorney General), 2022 FC 1503 at para 20; Lajoie v Canada (Attorney General), 2022 FC 1088 at para 12.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the decision and process were unfair; the standard of review is reasonableness, per prior cases.

propositions.text: Court must independently analyze procedural fairness of decision-maker's process.
propositions.quote: On issues relating to procedural fairness, the reviewing court must conduct its own analysis of the process followed by the decision-maker to determine whether the process was fair: Bharadwaj v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 1362 at para 8.

propositions.text: Review of procedural fairness is functionally correctness standard.
propositions.quote: This approach to review is functionally the same as applying the correctness standard: Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 at paras 49-56.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness owed to CERB and CRB applicants is low.
propositions.quote: The level of procedural fairness owed to CERB and CRB applicants is at the low end of the spectrum: Cozak v Canada (Attorney General), 2023 FC 1571 at para 17.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains procedural fairness review is correctness standard and low for CERB and CRB applicants.

propositions.text: CRA decision based on findings: CERB - income over $1,000, voluntary quit, no COVID-19 related work stoppage; CRB - voluntary quit, no 50% income reduction.
propositions.quote: As noted above, the CRA’s decision was based on the following findings: CERB Mr. Li earned more than $1,000 of employment or self-employment income during the applicable payment period. He quit his job voluntarily. He did not stop working or have his hours reduced for reasons related to COVID-19. CRB He quit his job voluntarily. He did not have a 50% reduction in his average weekly income compared to the previous year due to COVID-19.

paragraphs.summary: The CRA decision was based on findings about income, voluntary quitting, and lack of COVID-19 related work stoppage.

propositions.text: Respondent concedes errors in CERB income finding and CRB income reduction finding due to lack of income calculations.
propositions.quote: In his written argument, counsel for the Respondent conceded that the first of the above CERB findings, and the second of the above CRB findings were in error, as the Second Level Reviewer had not completed any income calculations.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent concedes errors in CERB income and CRB income reduction findings due to no income calculations.

propositions.text: Court questioned respondent about CRB Act provision on quitting employment after Sept 27, 2020.
propositions.quote: At the hearing into this matter, I turned the Respondent’s attention to paragraph 3(1)(k) of the CRB Act, which is one of the several eligibility criteria for receipt of CRB benefits.

propositions.text: Provision allows quitting employment after Sept 27, 2020 if reasonable.
propositions.quote: It essentially provides that a person is eligible for the stipulated benefits if they have not, on or after September 27, 2020, quit their employment or voluntarily ceased to work, unless it was reasonable to do so.

propositions.text: Applicant quit before Sept 27, 2020; court asked how reviewer could rely on resignation to deny CRB.
propositions.quote: Given that the Applicant quit his warehouse job before September 27, 2020, I asked the Respondent how the Second Level Reviewer could rely on Mr. Li’s resignation as a ground for denying his CRB benefits.

propositions.text: Respondent conceded that relying on resignation to deny CRB was unreasonable.
propositions.quote: To his credit, counsel for the Respondent conceded that this aspect of the Second Level Reviewer’s decision was also unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court questioned the respondent about CRB eligibility rules; respondent conceded denial based on resignation was unreasonable.

propositions.text: Respondent concedes both grounds for CRB denial were unreasonable and submits court should grant application on CRB findings.
propositions.quote: As it is now conceded that both grounds on which the Second Level Reviewer denied Mr. Li’s CRB benefits were unreasonable, counsel for the Respondent has amended his argument and submits that the Court should grant this application in respect of the CRB findings.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent concedes both CRB denial grounds were unreasonable and asks court to grant application on CRB findings.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review is granted regarding CRB findings as they are not justified under legal constraints, especially paragraph 3(1)(k) of CRB Act.
propositions.quote: I agree with the parties that this application for judicial review should be granted in respect of the CRB findings because these findings do not appear to be justified in light of the relevant legal constraints, most notably paragraph 3(1)(k) of the CRB Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court grants judicial review for CRB findings as unjustified under legal constraints, notably paragraph 3(1)(k) of the CRB Act.

propositions.text: The reviewer’s conclusion that the Applicant voluntarily quit and was ineligible for CERB was reasonable and fair.
propositions.quote: the Respondent maintains that the reviewer’s conclusion that the Applicant voluntarily quit his job and that, as such, he was not eligible for the CERB, was reasonable. The Respondent also maintains that this decision was arrived at in a fair manner.

propositions.text: The court agrees that the reviewer’s conclusion on voluntary quitting and CERB ineligibility was reasonable and fair.
propositions.quote: I agree.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues and court agrees that the reviewer’s conclusion on voluntary quitting and CERB ineligibility was reasonable and fair.

propositions.text: Paragraph 6(1)(a) of the CERB Act defines eligibility for income support payment related to COVID-19 work cessation for at least 14 consecutive days.
propositions.quote: Paragraph 6(1)(a) of the CERB Act is as follows: 6 (1) A worker is eligible for an income support payment if 6 (1) Est admissible à l’allocation de soutien du revenu le travailleur qui remplit les conditions suivantes : (a) the worker, whether employed or self-employed, ceases working for reasons related to COVID-19 for at least 14 consecutive days within the four-week period in respect of which they apply for the payment; and a) il cesse d’exercer son emploi — ou d’exécuter un travail pour son compte — pour des raisons liées à la COVID-19 pendant au moins quatorze jours consécutifs compris dans la période de quatre semaines pour laquelle il demande l’allocation; […] […]

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 6(1)(a) of the CERB Act defines eligibility for income support for COVID-19 related work cessation of at least 14 days.

propositions.text: Subsection 6(2) of the CERB Act excludes voluntary quitting from the definition of ceasing work under paragraph 6(1)(a).
propositions.quote: Thereafter, subsection 6(2) of the CERB Act narrows the scope of the word “ceases” for the purposes of paragraph 6(1)(a): (2) An employed worker does not cease work for the purpose of paragraph (1)(a) if they quit their employment voluntarily. (2) Pour l’application de l’alinéa (1)a), un travailleur ne cesse pas d’exercer son emploi s’il le quitte volontairement.

paragraphs.summary: Subsection 6(2) of CERB Act excludes voluntary quitting from ceasing work under paragraph 6(1)(a).

propositions.text: Applicant ceased work by voluntarily quitting; he was not terminated or temporarily laid off.
propositions.quote: While the Applicant ceased his work at the warehouse within the relevant CERB time period, it is clear that this work stopped because Mr. Li voluntarily quit his job. He was not terminated, and he was not temporarily laid off from this job.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Applicant voluntarily quit work; he was not terminated or laid off.

propositions.text: Applicant was not forthcoming with CRA about reason for leaving warehouse job, initially claiming layoff or job loss.
propositions.quote: On this point, I also note that in his interactions with CRA, Mr. Li does not appear to have been forthcoming on this point. For example, in a call with a CRA employee on September 25, 2024, Mr. Li is recorded as indicating that he was laid off from his warehouse job because he was deemed non-essential. As noted above, at another time, Mr. Li stated “I lost my job on July 17, 2020.” It was only during the Second Level Review, when the Applicant provided his ROE from the warehouse job, that it became clear that he had quit his job.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Applicant was not forthcoming with CRA, initially claiming layoff or job loss, but later shown to have quit.

propositions.text: Despite language barrier, Applicant conveyed inaccurate information to CRA about why he stopped working at warehouse.
propositions.quote: I understand that English is not Mr. Li’s first language (he communicated through an interpreter at the hearing in this matter). Nevertheless, it appears that he was able to convey information to CRA officials, and this information did not accurately reflect why he stopped working at the warehouse.

paragraphs.summary: Despite language barrier, Applicant conveyed inaccurate information to CRA about stopping warehouse work.

propositions.text: It was reasonable for Second Level Reviewer to conclude Applicant voluntarily quit, despite Applicant’s claim of fear and childcare reasons.
propositions.quote: In any event, it became clear before the Second Review was completed that the Applicant had quit his job. On this point, Mr. Li says that his resignation from the warehouse job was not “voluntary” in the sense that he would not have left the job if he had not been afraid of catching COVID-19, and if there had been childcare options available during the pandemic. True as this may be, it was reasonable in the circumstances for the Second Level Reviewer to conclude that Mr. Li had quit his job voluntarily: Bui v Canada (Attorney General), 2025 FC 1731 at paras 23-25; Phipps v Canada (Attorney General), 2025 FC 421 at paras 31-33.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it reasonable for Second Level Reviewer to conclude Applicant voluntarily quit despite his fear and childcare reasons.

propositions.text: Applicant argues process was unfair because First Review made no findings on resignation voluntariness, causing surprise at Second Review.
propositions.quote: Mr. Li argues that the process was unfair, primarily because over the course of the First Review, no findings were made related to his resignation from the warehouse job. As such, Mr. Li argues that he was taken by surprise by the Second Review decision and was not given adequate notice that this decision would turn on the question of the voluntariness of his departure from work.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues process was unfair due to no findings on resignation voluntariness in First Review, causing surprise at Second Review.

propositions.text: Applicant had several conversations with CRA, was explained process and eligibility criteria, and had fair opportunity to meet case.
propositions.quote: While I have some sympathy for this argument, the record indicates that Mr. Li had several conversations with CRA officials, and that the process was explained to him, including the general eligibility and income criteria. Given the level of procedural protections owed in this context, I find that Mr. Li had adequate notice of the case he had to meet and was provided with a fair opportunity to meet it.

propositions.text: Applicant’s misrepresentations to CRA do not support his claim of unfair treatment in review process.
propositions.quote: For the record, Mr. Li’s apparent misrepresentations to CRA officials as to how he left his warehouse job do not assist in his argument that he has been treated unfairly in the review process.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Applicant had adequate notice and fair opportunity despite some sympathy; misrepresentations do not support unfair treatment claim.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review dismissed for CERB decision, granted for CRB decision, remitted for redetermination by new decision-maker; no costs awarded.
propositions.quote: For the above reasons, the application for judicial review in respect of the CERB decision is dismissed. The application for judicial review in respect of the CRB decision is granted, and this matter alone will be returned to the CRA for redetermination by a new decision-maker. Owing to the Applicant’s mixed success on this application for judicial review, no costs will be awarded. JUDGMENT in T-3238-25 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The application for judicial review is granted in part. The application in respect of the Respondent’s decision under the Canada Emergency Response Benefit Act is dismissed. The application in respect of the Respondent’s decision under the Canada Recovery Benefit Act is granted and the matter is remitted for redetermination by a different reviewer. No costs are awarded.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses judicial review for CERB decision, grants it for CRB decision, remits for redetermination, and awards no costs.
